blocks.text: James,

The claim listing your team sent reconciles to the reinsurance statements for every year in the study except the most recent one. I believe the gap in that year is a question of timing rather than missing records, and I wanted to add that to Robert's note from yesterday before we go further.

The claims that do not yet appear on the statements were all incurred in the last few months of that year. That pattern fits statements that record a claim when it is settled, while the listing records it when it was incurred. If that is the explanation, nothing in the {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}} data needs correcting. We would put the two sources on the same basis and carry on.

Could someone on your team confirm which basis the statements use? A line or two is enough. Until we hear, we will leave that year out of the experience comparison rather than adjust it ourselves. The earlier years are unaffected, and we have drawn no conclusions from the experience so far, so nothing you have from us depends on the answer. Michelle and I are carrying on with the rest of the listing in the meantime.
Regards
Working Session: Reinsurance Pricing Review for {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}}

This was the working session we planned for the middle of the review. It had three purposes: to close the open data questions, to look at the first experience results, and to agree how the comparison with the proposed reinsurance rates will be made. No view on the proposed rates was reached or offered. Nothing below should be read as one.
Those attending
Where the data stand

Michelle Banks reported that the data checks are complete. The in-force listing ties to the policy counts and face amounts in the company's own records. The claim listing now ties to the reinsurance statements in every year. James Garcia confirmed that the statements record a claim when it is settled, not when it is incurred. That accounts for the shortfall Karen Harris found in the most recent year. We agreed to restore that year to the study on an incurred basis and to record the adjustment in the data summary.

Michelle also set out the extent of our reliance. We have checked the data for consistency and reasonableness. We have not audited them. The report will say so, and it will list the checks we made, as the actuarial standards of practice on data quality require.
First look at the experience

Karen Harris walked us through the first comparison of actual claims with the claims expected under the industry mortality table. What the data show is that claims at the younger issue ages have run below expected, and that the older ages are close to expected. There are few claims at the older ages, so the second observation carries less weight than the first.

How much weight the block's own experience should carry against the industry table is a judgment, not a measurement. Robert Lawrence said he will set out the approach in writing before any figure is used in the rate comparison, so that the choice can be read and questioned on its own. Karen will rerun the comparison once the restored year is in. Her exhibits will show the experience with and without that year.
The rate comparison

We then turned to the second half of the review. Karen will project the expected claim cost on the block under the assumption we settle on. Michelle will set that cost against the premiums the proposed rates would produce, by issue age and in total.

James Garcia asked whether our report would say if the rates are fair. Robert explained what the review can support. The report will say whether the proposed rates are reasonable in relation to the block's experience and the assumptions it states. It will not assess the reinsurer's expenses, its margin, or its financial strength, because none of the data we hold bears on those questions. James accepted that and asked that the report say it plainly. We agreed that it will.
The comparison has to be made against the full proposal. The rate schedule we hold covers only part of the issue age range, and James undertook to send the rest.
Actions agreed

rows: Send the complete rate schedule from the reinsurance proposal, covering every issue age
Restore the most recent year on an incurred basis and rerun the experience comparison
Issue the written data summary, including the adjustment to the most recent year
Set out in writing the approach to weighting the block's own experience against the industry table
Begin the comparison of expected claim cost with the proposed premiums

blocks.text: Corrections to these notes are welcome. Please send them to Robert Lawrence, and a revised copy will go to everyone who attended.
Reinsurance Pricing Review for {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}}
Status at the midpoint
Prepared by Karen Harris, Actuarial Associate, with Michelle Banks and Robert Lawrence.
Where the review stands

The review is on schedule and within its budget at the midpoint. The data work is finished, the experience study is complete, and we have begun the comparison with the proposed reinsurance rates. Nothing we have found so far changes the scope or the timetable in our engagement letter. We have not yet formed a view on the proposed rates, and this report offers none.
The rest of this report sets out what has been finished since the working session, what remains, and the points we think you should keep in view between now and the draft report.
Completed since the working session

Michelle Banks has issued the written data summary. It records the checks we made on the in-force listing and the claim listing, the reconciliation of claims to the reinsurance statements, and the one adjustment we made. Following your team's confirmation that the statements record a claim when it is settled, the most recent year is back in the study on an incurred basis. The summary also states the extent of our reliance. We checked the data for consistency and reasonableness. We did not audit them, and the report will say so in the same terms.

I have rerun the experience comparison with the restored year. The pattern described at the working session holds. Claims at the younger issue ages have run below what the industry mortality table predicts, and the older ages are close to expected. Adding the year made the younger-age result firmer. It did little for the older ages, where claims are still few. In checking the rerun I found a subtotal in one of our working exhibits that did not tie to the detail beneath it. The formula error was ours, it was caught before the exhibit left our office, and it does not affect anything described here.

Robert Lawrence has set out in writing how much weight the block's own experience will carry against the industry table at each age. That weighting is a judgment, and we have kept it apart from the experience results so it can be read and challenged on its own terms. It rests on the number of claims behind each age group. Where claims are few, the industry table carries most of the weight. We will send the note to you with the draft report, and we are glad to take you through it sooner if that would help.

Your team has also sent the complete rate schedule from the proposal, covering every issue age. The comparison now works from the full schedule, which was the last input we needed from you for the second half of the review.
The work ahead

What remains is the rate comparison itself and the report. I am projecting the expected claim cost on the block under the weighted assumption. Michelle is setting that cost against the premiums the proposed rates would produce, by issue age and in total. Once that is done we will test how far the result moves under reasonable alternative assumptions, so the report can show whether its conclusion depends on any one of them.

As agreed at the working session, the report will say whether the proposed rates are reasonable in relation to the block's experience and the assumptions the report states. It will not assess the reinsurer's expenses, its margin, or its financial strength. The draft goes through an internal review before it reaches you. Robert Lawrence will sign the final opinion once your comments on the draft have been addressed.
Risks and open questions

The thinness of the older-age experience is the main limit on what the report can say. For those ages the conclusion will rest more on the industry table than on the block's own claims, and the report will make that plain. This is not a risk to the timetable. It is a boundary on how firmly we can speak about the older ages. We raise it here so that it is not new to you when the draft arrives.

A revised proposal from the reinsurer would mean rerunning the comparison on the new terms. A revision to the rates alone can be absorbed within the current timetable. A change to the structure of the treaty, such as the retention or the share of each policy ceded, would take longer and could affect the fee. If that happens we will raise it with you before doing the work.

Some questions that reach us are related to this review, such as the accounting treatment of the reinsurance or its effect on the company's capital position. The data we hold cannot support an answer to them, and they are outside the scope of the engagement. When one comes up we will say so, and we can discuss a separate scope if the company wants that work done.
Fees and time

Our fee for the review is {{fact:f:E-2024-001.fee}}, as set out in the engagement letter. Time charged to date is in line with the work completed, and we expect to finish within the fee. The one development that could change this is a structural revision to the proposal, described above, and we would discuss it with you before any additional work began.

We are grateful for how quickly your team has answered our questions, which kept the data work short. Please send questions about this report to Karen Harris, or to Robert Lawrence on any matter of scope.
